content:
The Simple & Compound Interest chapter is a high-yield part of the CAT Quantitative Aptitude section, and a favourite in XAT, SNAP, NMAT and CMAT too. This guide explains what CAT Simple & Compound Interest tests, the formulas and shortcuts worth memorising, the mistakes that cost marks, and a free 10-question online test you can take right now.

Take the quiz below first, read the explanation for anything you miss, then use the chapter e-book at the end for full, exam-level practice.

What CAT asks on Simple & Compound Interest

Simple interest, compound interest (annual and more frequent), the CI–SI difference, and growth / depreciation.

Key formulas & shortcuts

  • SI = P·R·T/100; CI: A = P(1 + R/100)ᵀ.
  • For 2 years, CI − SI = P(R/100)².
  • Rule of 72: money doubles in about 72/R years.
  • For the same P, R, T, CI ≥ SI (equal only in year 1).

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using the SI formula where compounding is intended.
  • Forgetting to adjust R and T when compounding is half-yearly/quarterly.
  • Mixing up amount and interest.

questions.q: Find the difference between Simple Interest and Compound Interest on a sum of Rs. 10,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, where interest is compounded annually.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Simple Interest for 2 years at 10% = (10000 * 10 * 2) / 100 = Rs. 2000.
Step 2: Compound Interest for 2 years at 10% uses effective rate = 10 + 10 + (10*10)/100 = 21%.
Step 3: Compound Interest = 21% of 10000 = Rs. 2100.
Step 4: Difference = 2100 - 2000 = Rs. 100.

questions.q: A sum of money placed at compound interest doubles itself in 5 years. In how many years will it become 8 times of itself?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In compound interest, if a sum becomes k times in t years, it becomes kⁿ times in n × t years.
Step 2: Here, k = 2, t = 5 years.
Step 3: We need the amount to be 8 times, which is 2³ times ( n = 3 ).
Step 4: Total time = 3 × 5 = 15 years.
